translation: The Blessed Lord said: He who performs his prescribed, systemic duty (karyam karma) without leaning upon or depending on the fruits of action, is a genuine renunciant (Sannyasi) and a true practitioner of discipline (Yogi). One does not become a renunciant merely by relinquishing the domestic fire ritual (niragnih), nor does one become a Yogi simply by abandoning physical actions (akriyah).
simple_explanation: Medieval visual traditions created a false division in human society, presenting a Sannyasi as an idle wanderer in ochre robes who refuses to cook food or engage in labor, and a Yogi as someone sitting frozen with eyes closed, disconnected from community survival. Sri Krishna vigorously strikes down this misinterpretation. If a soldier on the borders leaves his post claiming he wants to cultivate non-violence, or if a magistrate leaves the bench to escape the emotional stress of sentencing criminals, their action is not renunciation—it is raw, self-centered desertion. Real renunciation is internal; it means executing your designated duty smoothly because it preserves cosmic balance, without constantly asking, "What is in this for me?"

translation: O Pandava! Know that what the sages call complete renunciation (Sannyasa), is identical to the path of selfless action (Yoga). For no one can ever become a true Yogi without thoroughly renouncing the thirst for personal, imaginative planning and reward-driven motives (sankalpa).

For a reflective seeker (Muni) who wishes to ascend to the peak of Yoga, active, selfless work (Karma) is declared to be the necessary stepping stone. But for that very same practitioner once he has successfully climbed and settled onto the peak of yoga (yogarudha), tranquility and serene meditation (shamah) are said to be the sustaining means.

When a practitioner develops such profound maturity that he is no longer enslaved by attraction toward sense objects, nor bound by personal attachments to his actions, and has completely discarded all reward-oriented mental designs (sarva-sankalpa-sannyasi), he is then declared to be firmly established on the peak of yoga (yogarudha).

An individual must elevate his lower self by the strength of his higher, rational Self, and never allow himself to sink into degradation or self-pity. For the Self alone is the truest friend of the individual, and the self alone can act as his most vicious enemy.
simple_explanation: This verse highlights the complete psychological self-reliance inherent in Vedic philosophy. No external agent, historical intermediary, or miraculous savior can step in to handle your mental training for you. Your lower, emotional, desire-driven mind (manas) must be firmly disciplined, reshaped, and raised by your higher, objective intellect (buddhi). If you surrender to your whims, you are self-sabotaging; if you conquer them, you unlock supreme internal freedom.

translation: The higher Self acts as a supportive friend to that individual who has successfully subdued and mastered his lower self through the intellect. But for one who has failed to control his inner faculties (anatmanah), his own unbridled mind remains locked in perpetual hostility against him, acting exactly like an external enemy.

To one who has fully conquered his lower self and achieved profound, unshakeable inner peace, his higher intellect remains completely unmoving, clear, and focused on the Supreme Divine amidst all earthly dualities—whether encountering biting cold or scorching heat, intense pleasure or agonizing pain, or public honor and stinging disgrace.

The Yogi whose heart is entirely satisfied with scriptural knowledge (Jnana) and direct, verified realization (Vijnana), who stands unmoving and resolute like an anvil (kutasthah), whose senses are thoroughly subdued, and to whom a clod of earth, a common stone, and a lump of pure gold hold equal value in terms of personal craving—he is declared to be fully integrated and enlightened (yuktah).

He who maintains an unswerving, balanced, and impartial intellect (sama-buddhih) toward a disinterested well-wisher (suhrid), an affectionate companion (mitra), an open adversary (ari), an indifferent onlooker (udasina), an arbitrator (madhyastha), a loathsome person (dveshya), relative clansmen (bandhu), as well as toward the highly virtuous and the deeply fallen sinners—he stands out as pre-eminent among human beings.

A practitioner of Yoga should constantly strive to concentrate his mind on the Divine, retiring periodically to a quiet, undisturbed space, staying alone, with his mental faculties and lower self tightly disciplined, entirely free from personal longings and untainted by any urge for possessiveness (aparigrahah).

In a naturally clean, hygienic, and spiritually pure location, he should set up a stable, firm seat for himself, which is neither excessively high nor inconveniently low, and cover it systematically with sacred Kusha grass, an insulating deer-skin sheet, and a soft, clean cloth on top.
simple_explanation: This verse details the foundational physics of a healthy, productive meditation environment. The seat must be insulated from the cold, damp ground using natural, non-conducting layers (kusha grass and cloth) to prevent the dispersion of bodily bio-currents during intense deep- breathing exercises (Pranayama). It must be steady, ensuring the body does not tumble or wobble when physical consciousness recedes.

translation: Seating himself firmly on that preparation, focusing his mind entirely on a single point, with the chaotic operations of his thoughts and sensory currents thoroughly brought to heel, he must practice meditation (Yoga) for the ultimate, absolute purification of his inner psyche (Atma-vishuddhaye).

Keeping his torso, neck, and head perfectly straight, unbending, and completely still, looking steady forward without casting his eyes around in different directions, focusing his attention inwardly as if fixing his gaze toward the tip of his own nose (nasikagram);
simple_explanation: “Looking at the tip of the nose” does not mean crossing one's eyeballs until a headache develops. In Sanskrit physiological grammar, it refers to focusing the mental awareness entirely on the respiratory root inside the nostrils where the Prana currents enter, preventing the optical nerves from collecting external visual distractions. The spine must remain straight to allow the central nervous column to function without compression.

translation: With a completely tranquilized mind, utterly purged of fear, anchored firmly in the sacred vow of self-restraint and celibacy (Brahmachari-vrate), keeping his thoughts tightly checked, he must sit with his consciousness focused on Me, looking upon Me alone as his absolute, ultimate goal.

Thus continuously training and keeping his mind integrated, the Yogi of systematically disciplined mind attains that supreme, absolute peace (Nirvana-paramam) which resides within My divine nature, terminating all worldly friction.

O Arjuna! This Yoga is impossible for one who overeats gluttonously, and it is equally impossible for one who tortures his body by starving himself completely. It is not unlocked by someone who sleeps excessively, nor can it ever be achieved by one who stays awake all night in forced vigils.
simple_explanation: Sri Krishna explicitly rejects all forms of neuro-destructive asceticism and self-mortification. The Vedic path is the path of elegant balance, anticipating the modern physiological understanding of health. Starving the brain or deprivated sleep damages the nervous system, destroying the higher intellectual capacity required for meditation.

translation: For him who is perfectly regulated in his diet and recreation (yukta-ahara-vihara), who maintains a balanced, disciplined exertion while performing his daily labor, and who keeps a strict rhythm in his hours of sleep and waking—to him alone does this Yoga become the destroyer of all worldly miseries and sorrows (dukhaha).

When the completely disciplined, well-trained mind settles smoothly down and remains anchored exclusively within the Self, thoroughly emancipated from cravings toward any type of objective desires, then is that practitioner declared to be truly integrated and established in yoga (yuktah).

Like the steady, unflickering flame of a lamp kept in a completely windless place—such is the classic, timeless analogy used by sages to describe the unmoving mind of a Yogi who is deeply absorbed in meditating upon the Self.

When the mind, thoroughly quieted through the systematic practice of Yoga, achieves supreme stillness; when, perceiving the higher Self by the light of the purified internal organ, the practitioner finds absolute satisfaction within the Self alone;

When he directly experiences that boundless, absolute bliss (atyantikam sukham) which belongs to the realm beyond the grasp of the physical senses and is perceived solely by the purified, razor-sharp intellect; and established in which, he never veers or slips away from the ultimate Reality;

Upon acquiring which, he evaluates no other worldly prize or gain as superior to it; and anchored securely in which, he is never shaken or disrupted even by the most colossal, crushing weight of earthly sorrow (gurunapi dukhena);

Let this complete, absolute severance from all contact with suffering (dukha-sanyoga- viyogam) be known by the definitive name of Yoga. This Yoga must be practiced with absolute steel resolve, accompanied by a resilient heart that refuses to succumb to despondency or fatigue.

Thoroughly abandoning, without leaving any hidden trace, all arbitrary desires born of speculative mental designs (sankalpa-prabhavan), and completely restraining the entire network of the senses from all sides by the sheer power of the disciplined mind;

Step by step, with meticulous patience (shanaih shanaih), he must guide his mind into absolute stillness using the intellect strengthened by unswerving fortitude (dhriti). Having securely anchored his mind within the Self, he must not allow it to chase any other objective thoughts.

Whichever way the highly flickering, restless, and unstable mind wanders outward chasing external stimuli, the practitioner must systematically pull it back from those specific directions, bringing it back repeatedly under the absolute control of the Self alone.

Supreme, unalloyed bliss spontaneously approaches this Yogi whose mind is completely tranquilized, whose passion-driven lower quality (Ragas) has been utterly neutralized, who is completely purged of sin, and who stands established in absolute union with the Divine (Brahma-bhutam).

Thus continuously keeping his faculties integrated, the Yogi, fully liberated from all moral taints, easily experiences the infinite, all-pervading bliss born of constant contact with the Divine Consciousness (Brahma-samsparsham).

He whose heart is fully integrated through Yoga and who looks upon all creation with a completely equal, impartial eye (sarvatra sama-darshinah), perceives his own higher Self as residing within every single living creature, and views all created beings as existing within his own expanded consciousness.
simple_explanation: This verse provides the philosophical foundation for global compassion and public duty. True meditation does not turn a person into a cold, isolated island. Instead, it systematically expands his boundary of selfhood. If he sees his own self in the entire nation, he works for the nation's liberation with the exact same natural intensity that a selfish man displays when feeding his individual stomach.

translation: He who perceives My divine presence operating everywhere throughout creation, and views everything as existing within Me—to him I am never lost or distant, and he is never lost or separated from Me.

That Yogi who, established firmly in this absolute unity, serves and honors Me as residing within all living creatures—he remains securely anchored within Me, no matter what external roles or duties he may be actively executing in the physical world.

O Arjuna! He who evaluates the pleasure or pain of every single living being by the exact same metric that he applies to himself (atmaupamyena), looking upon everyone's welfare with a completely equal eye—he is regarded by Me as the highest and most perfect of all Yogis.

Arjuna said: O Madhusudana! This system of Yoga based on absolute, unswerving equanimity which You have just declared to me—I am unable to see how it can have a stable, long-term footing in real life, owing to the extremely restless and volatile nature of the human mind.

For the mind is notoriously turbulent, O Krishna! It is aggressively chaotic (pramathi), immensely powerful, and stubbornly recalcitrant (dridham). Trying to bind it or bring it under permanent restraint seems to me as incredibly difficult as trying to arrest the wild, sweeping wind with my bare hands.

The Blessed Lord said: Without a shadow of doubt, O mighty-armed warrior, the mind is extraordinarily volatile and hard to restrain. But, O son of Kunti, it can be brought under complete mastery through consistent, scientific practice (Abhyasa) and the systematic cultivation of detachment (Vairagya).
simple_explanation: Krishna provides the definitive psychological formula for mind control, later echoed directly in Patanjali’s Yoga Sutra (1.12): “Abhyāsa-vairāgyābhyāṁ tannirodhaḥ”. Abhyasa means building constructive neural pathways by repeatedly steering the mind back to its duty. Vairagya means systematically starving negative habits by recognizing that running after fleeting sense objects always ends in exhaustion.

translation: For one whose mind is entirely undisciplined and wild, this state of Yoga is almost impossible to secure—such is My definitive view. But for the self-controlled person who strives systematically using the proper scientific methods (upayatah), its attainment is completely within reach.

Arjuna said: O Krishna! If a practitioner is endowed with genuine faith but lacks sufficient self-discipline, and his mind occasionally wanders away from the path of yoga before he can reach full perfection, what ultimate destination does he encounter upon failing to secure the peak of yoga?

Does he not, O mighty-armed Lord, lose his footing on both fronts, ending up utterly ruined like a scattered, broken cloud (chinnabhramiva)—having missed the temporary rewards of the material world on one hand, and failed to secure the spiritual realization of Brahman on the other?

Kindly destroy this agonizing doubt of mine completely, O Krishna! For there is absolutely no one else to be found besides You who possesses the transcendent capacity to slash through a doubt of this nature.

The Blessed Lord said: O Partha! Neither in this material world nor in the life hereafter does destruction or spiritual decay ever overtake such an earnest practitioner. For write this down as an absolute cosmic law, My beloved child (Tata): anyone who performs constructive, righteous work for the welfare of the world can never slide down into a miserable state of degradation (durgati).
simple_explanation: This verse highlights the unbreakable conservation of spiritual energy in the Vedic universe. No honest effort is ever erased or deleted from your karmic record. If death interrupts your spiritual practice mid-way, your accumulated mental conditioning (Samskaras) is securely carried forward into your next life, ensuring you pick up right where you left off.

translation: The practitioner who fell from the path of yoga (yoga-bhrashtah) ascends after death to the realms of the highly righteous, resides there for vast, comforting periods, and is eventually reborn on earth into a clean, ethically upright, and prosperous household (shuchinam shrimatam gehe).

Or he is born directly into a lineage of highly wise, deeply spiritual Yogis (dhimatam yoginam kule). To secure an extraordinary birth of this caliber in the human world is exceedingly rare and difficult.

In that fresh environment, O joy of the Kurus, he automatically reconnects with the precise intellectual intuition and spiritual orientation developed in his previous body (paurva- dehikam buddhi-sanyogam), and he spontaneously begins to strive with even greater momentum toward ultimate perfection.

Driven forward helplessly by the sheer momentum of his previous life's training, he is irresistibly drawn back to spiritual discipline. Even a basic seeker who merely desires to know the science of Yoga rises far above the superficial ritualistic rewards outlined in the literal Vedic texts (shabda-brahma).

Striving with intense, systematic dedication, entirely purged of all moral impurities and mental weaknesses over the course of multiple lifetimes, the Yogi achieves ultimate perfection and ascends directly to the supreme Goal.

A Yogi is superior to the physical ascetics who perform bodily mortifications (tapasvis); he is also superior to the mere theoretical scholars who carry bookish knowledge (jnanis); and he stands far above the reward-driven ritualists who perform actions for personal profit (karmis). Therefore, O Arjuna, shake off your dejection and become a true Yogi!

And of all the various classes of Yogis, he who honors and worships Me with his innermost self completely absorbed in My divine presence, and who is endowed with unshakeable faith—he is evaluated by Me as the most perfectly integrated and deeply united of all.
